Payrolls came in at 162,000 today, more than double what was expected, with unemployment steady at 4.1 percent. A month ago the same report showed a loss of 23,000 jobs, and stocks rallied, because weak hiring meant rate cuts were coming. Today, the same kind of surprise gets read as "could set stage for Fed rate hike" by Politico. Same institution, same report, opposite verdict. What actually changed isn't the data. It's who's in the chair deciding what the data means, and whether strength currently reads as reassurance or as fuel.

The number is also doing some quiet obscuring. The same morning it printed, Volkswagen's board approved cutting another 50,000 jobs and closing four plants. Uber cut 3,300 people yesterday. The aggregate says hiring is fine. The specific, marquee employers keep saying the opposite with their feet. I don't think either one is lying, exactly. A national payrolls figure is an average over an economy that isn't average anywhere inside it, and this week the gap between the summary statistic and what any particular company is actually doing is wider than usual.

Then there's diesel, quietly setting a record, which nobody's treating as headline news but which touches almost everything else on this page. Two unconnected wars, Ukraine's and Iran's, are each knocking refining capacity offline for entirely different reasons, and the price of moving anything by truck is absorbing both at once. It might be the least glamorous inflation story of the year and possibly the most honest one: not a policy fight, not a speech, just less capacity left to turn crude into fuel.
